draft.title: Monohybrid crosses
card: A monohybrid cross follows one gene with two alleles. A Punnett square shows the gametes (sex cells) of each parent along the sides and the possible offspring genotypes inside the boxes.
Each parent gives one allele to each gamete. A heterozygous parent, such as Bb, makes two kinds of gamete, B and b, in equal numbers.
Two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb) give offspring genotypes in the ratio 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb. If B is completely dominant, the phenotype ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
The square gives probabilities for each offspring, not a guarantee. Each fertilisation is a separate chance event, so a small family may not match the ratio.
draft.remember: A Punnett square predicts the chance of each outcome. It does not fix the result for any one child.

a.q: Two pea plants that are both Tt are crossed. T is completely dominant over t. What fraction of offspring are expected to show the recessive trait?
a.why: Only the tt offspring show the recessive trait, and the square has one tt box out of four. Three quarters is tempting, but that is the share showing the dominant trait.
a.clue: Which genotype shows the recessive trait, and how many boxes is it?

b.q: Two heterozygous parents in Geelong each carry one allele for a recessive condition. They have three children, all unaffected. What is the chance that their fourth child is affected?
opts: Zero, as the ratio is already filled
b.why: Each child is a separate chance event, so the chance stays 1 in 4 for every birth. The ratio does not run out after three children, so the first three do not change the fourth.
b.clue: Does a past fertilisation change the next one?
